prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur. A live dinosaur has just been found in Africa and will be auctioned off. There is only one. Your client would like to buy the dinosaur and use it as the centerpiece in a new animal-themed park he would like to open. The park will be located in a major metropolitan area in a developed, Western country.
prompt.question:
This case is given in three parts. Address each in sequence:
1. What is the maximum price that our client should bid for the dinosaur?
2. How should the park be designed to maximize profits?
3. Our client will need to go to the financial markets to raise capital to build the park. How would you determine an appropriate discount rate?

clarifying_info.q: Where will the park be located?
clarifying_info.a: In a major metropolitan area in a developed, Western country.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have data on visitor demand, ticket prices, or costs?
clarifying_info.a: No specific data is provided. Push the candidate to make reasonable assumptions for all data needed.

clarifying_info.q: Is there competition from other dinosaur parks?
clarifying_info.a: There is only one live dinosaur in the world, so demand is effectively unlimited — visitor count is constrained by capacity, not demand.

exhibits.title: Case Text Page
exhibits.shows: The printed case page containing the problem statement and questions for this case
exhibits.data: No numerical data exhibit; the page contains the case narrative and three questions

framework: Determine maximum bid price by calculating the NPV of all future profits from the park
Revenue = (number of visitors x ticket price) + ancillary sales (food, souvenirs, marketing promotions, etc.)
Costs = Fixed costs (facility construction, dinosaur purchase price) + Variable costs (staffing, maintenance, operations)
Because demand is virtually unlimited (only one live dinosaur exists), visitor count is capacity-constrained — maximizing capacity is the primary lever
Use Little's Law (R = I x T) to model throughput and determine optimal park layout
For discount rate: identify benchmarks from companies/industries with a key asset of indeterminate life, since the dinosaur's lifespan is unknown

questions.prompt: What is the maximum price the client should bid for the dinosaur?
questions.guidance: The maximum bid equals the NPV of all future profits attributable to the dinosaur. Candidate should structure: Revenue (visitors x ticket + ancillary) minus Costs (fixed + variable), then discount cash flows. Since demand is unlimited, the binding constraint is capacity. Candidate should make explicit assumptions: e.g., ticket price ~$50, 5,000 visitors/day, 365 days/year, 30-year horizon, appropriate discount rate. The bid price = PV(future profits) — any value paid above this destroys value.

math.setup: Max bid = NPV of future park profits. Revenue = (daily visitors x ticket price + ancillary revenue per visitor) x operating days/year. Profit = Revenue - Variable costs - Fixed costs (excluding dinosaur purchase). Discount at WACC.
steps: Assume: 5,000 visitors/day, ticket price $50, ancillary $20/visitor, 365 days/year
At a 10% discount rate, PV of perpetuity = $61.25M / 0.10 = $612.5M
Max bid ≈ $612M (candidate's numbers will vary; logic and structure are key)
math.answer: Maximum bid price ≈ NPV of future profits; with illustrative assumptions approximately $600M+ (exact answer depends on candidate assumptions, which should be reasonable and clearly stated)

questions.prompt: How should the park be designed to maximize profits?
questions.guidance: Because demand is virtually unlimited, profit maximization reduces to capacity maximization. Candidate should propose and sketch multiple layout alternatives (e.g., linear path, circular loop, multiple viewing areas) and calculate throughput for each using Little's Law: R = I / T, where R = throughput (visitors/unit time), I = average number of visitors in the system, T = average time per visitor. The 'best' design maximizes R subject to safety/experience constraints. There is no single right answer — evaluation of alternatives and a defensible recommendation matter.

math.setup: Little's Law: R = I / T. R = throughput (visitors per hour), I = average inventory (visitors in exhibit at once), T = average time each visitor spends.
steps: Example: If exhibit holds I = 500 people and average visit time T = 30 minutes = 0.5 hours
Daily capacity = 1,000 x 10 operating hours = 10,000 visitors/day
Compare alternative layouts by solving for R under different I and T assumptions
math.answer: Design that maximizes R = I/T subject to visitor experience and safety constraints; candidate should evaluate at least two layout alternatives and recommend the highest-throughput option

questions.prompt: How would you determine an appropriate discount rate to raise capital from financial markets?
questions.guidance: Candidate should acknowledge that a standard WACC calculation is difficult because the dinosaur's lifespan is indeterminate (unknown). The recommended methodology is benchmarking: find companies or industries where the key asset also has an uncertain or indeterminate life (e.g., entertainment parks, zoos, biological research assets, oil/gas reserves). Use their observed cost of capital as a proxy, adjusting for size, leverage, and unique risk. Candidate should also mention the risk premium warranted by the dinosaur's unique/novel nature.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the park design consider to maximize both capacity and revenue?

categories.name: Layout & Flow
ideas: Linear vs. circular paths to control visitor flow
Multiple simultaneous viewing zones to spread demand
Timed entry tickets to smooth arrivals

categories.name: Cost Management
ideas: Optimize staffing levels by time of day
Efficient dinosaur enclosure design to minimize maintenance

categories.name: Risk Factors
ideas: Regulatory and safety requirements for a novel animal
Reputational risk if animal welfare is questioned

recommendation: Bid up to the NPV of the park's future profits (candidate-calculated figure), ensuring the purchase price does not exceed discounted cash flows
Design the park to maximize throughput using Little's Law, selecting the layout with highest R = I/T while maintaining visitor experience
Use industry benchmarking against assets with indeterminate life spans to set the discount rate
risks: Dinosaur lifespan is unknown — profits could terminate suddenly, significantly reducing NPV
Regulatory hurdles for housing a live dinosaur may raise costs or delay opening
Public or animal-welfare backlash could suppress demand
next_steps: Commission a feasibility study on site selection and construction costs
Consult with zoologists/paleontologists to estimate dinosaur lifespan and care requirements
Identify comparable public attractions to calibrate WACC benchmarks
Develop a phased capital-raising plan for park construction
